reference.source: Williams Obstetrics / Novak's Gynecology / Campbell-Walsh Urology
clinicalPearls: Cervical incompetence is painless progressive cervical dilatation in the second trimester leading to mid-trimester pregnancy loss or spontaneous preterm birth in the absence of contractions or labour
The hallmark history is recurrent second-trimester losses that are painless, often with rupture of membranes or bulging membranes and rapid, non-laborious delivery
Risk factors include previous cervical surgery (cone biopsy, large loop excision), cervical trauma from dilatation, congenital collagen or Mullerian abnormalities, and prior mechanical dilatation
Transvaginal ultrasound measurement of cervical length is the key surveillance tool, with progressive shortening and funnelling of the internal os indicating risk
Cervical cerclage, a stitch placed to reinforce the cervix, is offered based on history, ultrasound findings, or examination findings depending on the clinical scenario
Vaginal progesterone is used to reduce preterm birth risk in women with a short cervix, and can complement or substitute for cerclage in selected cases
History-indicated cerclage is typically placed electively in early second trimester, whereas ultrasound- or examination-indicated (rescue) cerclage is placed when shortening or dilatation is detected
Emergency rescue cerclage on a dilated cervix with exposed membranes carries higher risks of membrane rupture and infection and requires careful case selection
The diagnosis is clinical and somewhat retrospective, as no single definitive test confirms it, so it must be distinguished from preterm labour and infection
reference.pathophysiology: The cervix normally remains firm and closed under load until term, maintained by its collagen-rich connective tissue. In cervical insufficiency, structural or functional weakness of this tissue, whether congenital, from collagen disorders, or acquired through surgical or traumatic disruption, means the cervix cannot withstand the increasing mechanical stress of the growing pregnancy. It shortens, effaces, and dilates painlessly. As the cervix opens, the fetal membranes prolapse into the vagina, becoming exposed to ascending flora; membrane rupture and mid-trimester loss or preterm delivery follow, often without the coordinated contractions of true labour.
additionalDifferentials: Antiphospholipid syndrome and other causes of recurrent mid-trimester loss
additionalInvestigations: Serial transvaginal ultrasound cervical length measurement with assessment for funnelling
Speculum examination to assess dilatation and detect bulging or ruptured membranes
Screening for infection including genital and urinary cultures where relevant
Review of obstetric and surgical history for prior losses and cervical procedures
Assessment for alternative causes of recurrent loss such as thrombophilia or uterine anomaly where indicated
redFlags: Painless cervical dilatation with bulging or exposed fetal membranes in the second trimester
Rupture of membranes at previable or early gestation
Signs of intra-amniotic infection (fever, uterine tenderness, offensive discharge, maternal or fetal tachycardia)
Rapidly progressive cervical shortening on surveillance scanning
Onset of contractions or bleeding suggesting labour or abruption rather than pure insufficiency
reference.prognosis: With recognition and appropriate intervention, whether cerclage, progesterone, or close surveillance, many women achieve substantially prolonged gestation and improved neonatal outcomes in subsequent pregnancies. Prognosis is poorer when membranes are already prolapsed or ruptured, or when infection supervenes. Recurrence risk in future pregnancies is significant, warranting proactive planning.
pitfalls: Attributing painless mid-trimester loss to bad luck and not investigating for insufficiency
Placing a rescue cerclage without recognising established infection or advanced labour
Overlooking infection as either a cause or a contraindication to intervention
Relying on a single cervical length measurement rather than trends
Failing to plan surveillance or cerclage early in a subsequent at-risk pregnancy
management: Offer cervical cerclage, whether history-, ultrasound- or examination-indicated as a rescue stitch, to reinforce the cervix
Prescribe vaginal progesterone to reduce preterm birth risk in women with a short cervix
Undertake serial transvaginal ultrasound cervical length surveillance with assessment for funnelling in at-risk pregnancies
Advise activity modification, evaluate symptoms promptly and screen for and treat genital and urinary infection
Consider a cervical pessary as an alternative in selected cases
Give antenatal corticosteroids for foetal lung maturity and magnesium sulphate for neuroprotection if preterm delivery threatens
Provide multidisciplinary maternal-foetal medicine care and pre-pregnancy counselling, planning cerclage in future pregnancies
